name: Pump water
summary: Use 12V pumps made to run off a battery: RV water pumps, boat bilge pumps and car washer pumps. A small solar panel can drive a 12V pump directly while the sun shines, filling a raised tank that then feeds by gravity. Put the pump down by the water and push uphill, because suction lifts water only so far: about 6 m (20 ft) for a shallow-well pump (Wisconsin DNR DG-022), and one jet-pump maker caps total suction lift, pipe losses included, at 7.6 m (25 ft) at sea level and less at altitude (A.Y. McDonald jet pumps). If the source is above you, a siphon needs no pump at all.

parts.why: The pump itself: RV, bilge, washer and sump pumps
Pipe from the source to the tank; wider pipe loses less flow
Drives a 12V pump directly in sun
A raised tank stores pumped water for gravity feed
Runs the pump at night or in cloud
Float switches stop the pump when the tank is full
A check valve keeps the pipe primed when the pump stops

tips: Bilge pumps move lots of water at low lift but lose flow as the lift grows: Rule's 1500 model moves about 3,980 L an hour with no lift, 3,600 at 1 m and 1,950 at 2 m, where its chart stops; its bigger models keep about two-thirds to three-quarters at 2 m (Rule bilge 1500-4000).
RV and boat diaphragm pumps lift higher and prime themselves; most other small pumps don’t.
Pump by day into a raised tank. A tank 3 m up gives gentle pressure all night.
Screen the intake: one leaf or pebble can wreck a small pump.

Don't pipe drinking water through ordinary garden hose: the vinyl and brass fittings can hold lead. Use hose marked "drinking water safe" or NSF/ANSI 61 (sold for RVs and boats), and run it a few seconds first.

sources.title: Wisconsin DNR DG-022: Wisconsin Department of Natural Resources, Driven Point (Sand Point) Wells (PUB-DG-022, 2024)
